analysis.one_liner: Slaps a 25% tax on handguns, assault weapons, and ammunition, raises gun-dealer fees, and spends the money on hospitals treating gunshot victims.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or even a cosponsor — it died in committee at the end of the 104th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Representative Carrie Meek's bill would have raised the federal excise tax on handguns, assault weapons, and their ammunition to 25%, added a 25% tax on retail sales of those weapons, and raised the federal firearms dealer license fee from about $30 for three years to $2,500 a year. The money would flow into a new Health Care Trust Fund paying grants to not-for-profit hospitals and trauma centers that absorb large unpaid bills for treating gunshot victims. The bill cites federal findings that firearms injuries cost the health system over $4 billion a year and that public funds cover about 85% of hospitalization costs for gunshot victims. It was introduced, referred to three committees and two subcommittees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospitals and trauma centers that treat gunshot victims without being paid, and the taxpayers and insured patients who currently absorb those costs through cost-shifting. If higher prices discouraged some purchases, communities with high rates of gun violence would benefit from fewer shootings.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals and trauma centers that treat uninsured gunshot victims would get grants to offset uncompensated care costs they currently absorb.

The bill cites federal data that public funds already pay roughly 85% of hospitalization costs for firearm injuries, so shifting some of that cost to the gun trade reduces the burden on taxpayers and helps keep trauma centers financially solvent.

Higher taxes on handguns, assault weapons, large-capacity magazines, and their ammunition would raise prices on the products most associated with injury and death, which can reduce purchases at the margin.

analysis.who_pays: Buyers of handguns and assault weapons, who would pay a 25% federal excise tax on the products and their ammunition at the manufacturer and retail level, and licensed gun dealers, whose annual fee would jump from up to $90 for three years to $2,500 per year.
analysis.who_pays_short: Handgun and assault-weapon buyers, gun dealers

drawbacks.text: The 25% excise tax would fall on retail buyers, meaning higher prices on every handgun and assault-weapon purchase — a cost that hits lawful purchasers, not just criminals.
Raising the dealer license fee from up to $90 for three years to $2,500 per year would sharply increase costs for small gun dealers, likely pushing many low-volume dealers out of business.

The bill's broad 'assault weapon' definition, based on magazine capacity and concealability, would sweep in many common firearms and large-capacity magazines, a definition critics have long argued is unworkably broad.
Trust Fund money would only be available 'as provided in appropriations Acts,' so Congress could collect the taxes and fees yet decline to actually pay out grants to hospitals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea was coherent: a product whose known societal costs include billions in trauma-care bills would help pay for those costs. The costs fell on gun buyers and small dealers through higher prices and fees, and the bill was vague on the details — it left the tax structure, definitions, and administration to be worked out, and relied on annual appropriations to actually release Trust Fund money. As drafted, a 25% tax would fall partly on cheaper handguns used by lower-income owners, and the dealer fee increase could squeeze small rural dealers. Those are real costs, but the bill never advanced far enough for them to be tested; it died without a markup or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: One sponsor introduced it, not a single colleague signed on, no committee ever held a hearing, and the bill quietly expired when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Carrie Meek introduced the Firearm Victims Prevention Act of 1996 on January 23, 1996.
It attracted zero cosponsors in the House.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means, Judiciary, and Commerce Committees; the Commerce Health Subcommittee and the Judiciary Crime Subcommittee took jurisdiction, and neither acted on it.
No hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion is recorded; the bill expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun and ammunition manufacturers and retailers never faced the new taxes or fees, and gun dealers kept paying $30 instead of $2,500 a year. Hospitals and taxpayers continue to absorb the cost of gunshot-wound care.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers and dealers; hospitals keep absorbing costs

for.name: Rep. Carrie P. Meek
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a vote or even a cosponsor, so no party split on its merits was ever recorded; its sponsor was a Democrat in a Republican-controlled 104th Congress.

industries.note: The bill raised the manufacturers' excise tax on handguns, assault weapons, and their ammunition to 25%, directly cutting into sales margins. It targeted the exact products the industry makes most of its money on.

Retailers would owe a new 25% tax on every subsequent sale and dealers would pay $2,500 a year instead of about $30, sharply raising the cost of operating a gun store. Lawful dealers would bear the compliance burden even though the bill's targets were the consequences of gun violence.

Not-for-profit hospitals and trauma centers that absorb large unpaid bills for treating gunshot victims would receive dedicated grant funding. That money currently comes from taxpayers, insured patients through cost-shifting, or goes unpaid entirely.
